en: Good morning everyone, today I will walk you through our quarterly results.
tamil: அனைவருக்கும் காலை வணக்கம், இன்னைக்கு நம்ம காலாண்டு முடிவுகளை உங்களுக்கு விளக்கப் போறேன்.
explain: 'Walk you through' means explain step by step. 'I will' announces what you are going to do.
usage: Use it to start a presentation to colleagues or a manager.
leelaQ: How do you usually start a presentation at work?
answer: I usually greet everyone and tell them what I will cover.

en: Let me start with a quick overview before we go into the details.
tamil: விவரங்களுக்கு போறதுக்கு முன்னாடி ஒரு சின்ன மேலோட்டத்தோட ஆரம்பிக்கிறேன்.
context: Structuring the start of a talk.
explain: 'Let me' politely says what you will do next. It helps the audience follow your talk.
usage: Use it in a meeting or presentation to introduce the outline.
leelaQ: How do you organise a short talk for your team?
answer: I give a quick overview first and then explain the details.

en: As you can see on this slide, sales have grown by twenty percent.
tamil: இந்த ஸ்லைடுல பார்க்கிற மாதிரி, விற்பனை இருபது சதவீதம் அதிகரிச்சிருக்கு.
context: Pointing to a chart during a presentation.
explain: 'As you can see' draws attention to a visual. 'Have grown' links past growth to now.
usage: Use it when you show a chart or figure to an audience.
leelaQ: What good news did you share at your last meeting?
answer: I shared that our sales have grown this year.

en: That brings me to my next point, which is the budget.
tamil: அது என்னை அடுத்த விஷயத்துக்கு கொண்டு வருது, அது பட்ஜெட்.
context: Moving to the next topic in a talk.
explain: 'That brings me to' is a smooth link between two topics in a presentation.
usage: Use it to move from one topic to the next while presenting.
leelaQ: How do you move from one topic to another when you speak?
answer: I say that brings me to my next point.

en: To sum up, we need more time, more people and a clearer plan.
tamil: சுருக்கமா சொன்னா, நமக்கு அதிக நேரம், அதிக ஆட்கள், தெளிவான திட்டம் வேணும்.
context: Ending a presentation with a summary.
explain: 'To sum up' signals the final summary. Three items in a list sound strong and clear.
usage: Use it at the end of a talk or report to repeat the main message.
leelaQ: How do you end a presentation?
answer: I end by saying to sum up and repeating the main points.

en: Does anyone have any questions before I move on?
tamil: நான் அடுத்ததுக்கு போறதுக்கு முன்னாடி யாருக்காவது கேள்வி இருக்கா?
context: Checking with the audience during a talk.
explain: This question gives the audience a chance to speak. 'Move on' means go to the next part.
usage: Use it in the middle of a presentation or training session.
leelaQ: When do you ask your audience for questions?
answer: I ask after each main part so nobody feels lost.

en: I would like to thank you all for your time and attention.
tamil: உங்க எல்லாரோட நேரத்துக்கும் கவனத்துக்கும் நன்றி சொல்ல விரும்பறேன்.
explain: 'I would like to' is a polite, formal way to say what you want to do.
usage: Use it as the last line of a formal presentation or speech.
leelaQ: What do you say at the end of a speech?
answer: I thank everyone for their time and attention.

en: Could you please speak a little louder? We cannot hear you at the back.
tamil: கொஞ்சம் சத்தமா பேச முடியுமா? பின்னாடி எங்களுக்கு கேக்கல.
context: Asking a speaker to be louder.
explain: 'Could you please' is very polite. Giving a reason makes the request easier to accept.
usage: Use it in a hall or online meeting when the speaker is hard to hear.
leelaQ: What would you say if you could not hear a speaker?
answer: I would politely ask the speaker to speak a little louder.

en: I'm afraid I haven't finished the slides yet, but I'll share them tomorrow.
tamil: மன்னிக்கணும், நான் இன்னும் ஸ்லைடுகளை முடிக்கல, ஆனா நாளைக்கு அனுப்பறேன்.
context: Admitting that work is not ready.
explain: 'I'm afraid' softens bad news. 'Haven't finished yet' shows something is still in progress.
usage: Use it with a manager when your work is not ready on time.
leelaQ: What do you say when your work is not ready?
answer: I say I am sorry and promise to send it tomorrow.

en: Let's take a five-minute break and come back at eleven.
tamil: அஞ்சு நிமிஷம் இடைவேளை எடுத்துட்டு பதினொரு மணிக்கு திரும்ப வரலாம்.
context: Suggesting a break in a long session.
explain: 'Let's' makes a suggestion for the whole group. It sounds friendly, not bossy.
usage: Use it when you lead a long meeting or workshop.
leelaQ: When do you take a break in a long meeting?
answer: I suggest a short break after an hour so everyone feels fresh.

en: I truly believe this new system will save us a lot of time.
tamil: இந்த புது சிஸ்டம் நமக்கு நிறைய நேரத்தை மிச்சப்படுத்தும்னு நான் உண்மையா நம்பறேன்.
context: Persuading your team to try a new tool.
explain: 'I truly believe' adds strong feeling. 'Will save' gives a clear promise about the future.
usage: Use it when you try to convince colleagues or a boss about an idea.
leelaQ: What idea would you like to convince your team about?
answer: I want to convince them to use a simpler system.

en: If we start now, we will finish before the festival rush.
tamil: இப்போ ஆரம்பிச்சா, பண்டிகை கூட்டத்துக்கு முன்னாடி முடிச்சிடலாம்.
context: Convincing a partner to start early.
explain: This is a first conditional: if + present, will + verb. It shows a likely result.
usage: Use it to show the benefit of acting early.
leelaQ: Why is it good to start a task early?
answer: If I start early, I will finish without stress.

en: Think about how much money we could save every month.
tamil: மாசா மாசம் எவ்வளவு பணம் மிச்சப்படுத்தலாம்னு யோசிச்சு பாருங்க.
explain: 'Think about' invites the listener to imagine a benefit. 'Could' shows a possibility.
usage: Use it to persuade a family member or a customer.
leelaQ: How do you convince someone to save money?
answer: I ask them to think about how much they could save every month.

en: Why don't we try it for one month and then decide?
tamil: ஒரு மாசம் முயற்சி பண்ணிட்டு அப்புறம் முடிவு பண்ணலாமே?
context: Suggesting a small trial to a hesitant person.
explain: 'Why don't we' is a friendly suggestion. A trial period lowers the other person's fear.
usage: Use it when someone is unsure and you want them to agree to a small step.
leelaQ: What would you say to someone who is unsure about a new idea?
answer: I would ask why we don't try it for one month first.

en: I'm confident that our product will meet your needs.
tamil: எங்க தயாரிப்பு உங்க தேவைகளை பூர்த்தி செய்யும்னு நான் நம்பிக்கையா இருக்கேன்.
context: Talking to a customer about a product.
explain: 'I'm confident that' shows strong belief. It builds trust with a customer.
usage: Use it when selling or recommending something to a client.
leelaQ: How do you build trust with a customer?
answer: I speak honestly and say I am confident about my product.

en: Many of our customers have told us that it makes their work easier.
tamil: எங்க நிறைய வாடிக்கையாளர்கள் இது அவங்க வேலையை எளிதாக்குதுன்னு சொல்லியிருக்காங்க.
explain: Quoting other people is a strong way to persuade. 'Have told' shows past feedback that still matters.
usage: Use it in a sales talk to show that others are already happy.
leelaQ: What do customers say about your favourite shop?
answer: They say the staff are helpful and the prices are fair.

en: Wouldn't it be better to fix this problem now than to pay more later?
tamil: இப்போவே இந்த பிரச்சனையை சரி பண்றது, அப்புறம் அதிகம் செலவு பண்றதை விட நல்லதில்லையா?
context: Arguing for fixing a problem early.
explain: A 'wouldn't it' question makes the listener agree. 'Than' compares two choices.
usage: Use it to convince a manager or family member to act early.
leelaQ: Do you agree that fixing problems early is better?
answer: Yes, I agree because small problems become big if we wait.

en: You may not like the idea at first, but please hear me out.
tamil: முதல்ல இந்த யோசனை உங்களுக்கு பிடிக்காம இருக்கலாம், ஆனா தயவுசெஞ்சு நான் சொல்றதை கேளுங்க.
context: Asking a doubtful listener to be patient.
explain: 'Hear me out' means listen to everything I say before you judge.
usage: Use it when you know someone will resist your idea.
leelaQ: What do you say when you want someone to listen fully?
answer: I say please hear me out before you decide.

en: Our offer is only valid until Friday, so I would suggest deciding soon.
tamil: எங்க சலுகை வெள்ளிக்கிழமை வரைக்கும்தான், அதனால சீக்கிரம் முடிவு பண்ணுங்கன்னு சொல்வேன்.
context: Gently creating urgency with a customer.
explain: 'I would suggest' is a polite way to push. 'Valid until' tells the end date of an offer.
usage: Use it with a client when an offer or price will end soon.
leelaQ: What would you say if an offer is ending soon?
answer: I would tell the customer the offer is valid only until Friday.

en: Let me give you three good reasons why this plan works.
tamil: இந்த திட்டம் ஏன் வேலை செய்யும்னு மூணு நல்ல காரணங்கள் சொல்றேன்.
explain: Saying the number of reasons first helps listeners follow your argument.
usage: Use it in a meeting when you present your case.
leelaQ: Can you give me one reason to exercise daily?
answer: It keeps me healthy and gives me more energy.

en: Is there any room to lower the price a little?
tamil: விலையை கொஞ்சம் குறைக்க வாய்ப்பு இருக்கா?
explain: 'Room' here means possibility. It is a soft way to ask for a discount.
usage: Use it when you bargain with a vendor or supplier.
leelaQ: How do you ask for a better price politely?
answer: I ask if there is any room to lower the price.

en: We can agree to this price if you deliver by the fifth.
tamil: ஐந்தாம் தேதிக்குள்ள டெலிவரி பண்ணா இந்த விலைக்கு ஒத்துக்கலாம்.
explain: 'If' sets a condition. Negotiation often exchanges one benefit for another.
usage: Use it when you agree to a deal only with a condition.
leelaQ: What condition would you put in a deal?
answer: I would agree if they deliver on time.

en: That is a bit higher than we expected, to be honest.
tamil: உண்மையா சொன்னா, இது நாங்க எதிர்பார்த்ததை விட கொஞ்சம் அதிகம்.
context: Reacting to a price that seems high.
explain: 'A bit' and 'to be honest' soften your disagreement but keep the message clear.
usage: Use it when a quotation is more than your budget.
leelaQ: How do you react when a price is too high?
answer: I politely say it is higher than I expected.

en: Let's meet in the middle and settle at fifty thousand.
tamil: நடுவுல சந்திச்சு ஐம்பதாயிரத்துல முடிச்சிக்கலாம்.
explain: 'Meet in the middle' means each side gives a little. 'Settle' means reach a final deal.
usage: Use it when both sides are close but not yet agreed.
leelaQ: When is a compromise a good idea?
answer: It is good when both sides want the deal to happen.

en: We would be happy to continue if the terms are fair for both sides.
tamil: நிபந்தனைகள் இரண்டு பக்கத்துக்கும் நியாயமா இருந்தா தொடர்றதுல எங்களுக்கு சந்தோஷம்.
context: Showing interest but stating a condition.
explain: 'Would be happy to' is polite and formal. 'Terms' means the conditions of a deal.
usage: Use it in business talks to keep the door open.
leelaQ: What makes a deal fair for both people?
answer: Both people should gain something and feel respected.

en: I'm sorry, but that is the best offer we can make at this stage.
tamil: மன்னிக்கணும், இந்த நிலைமையில எங்களால கொடுக்கக்கூடிய சிறந்த சலுகை இதுதான்.
explain: 'I'm sorry, but' softens a refusal. 'At this stage' leaves a small chance to change later.
usage: Use it to say no to a lower price without sounding rude.
leelaQ: How do you say no politely in a negotiation?
answer: I say sorry and explain that it is my best offer.

en: Could you put that in writing so we are both clear?
tamil: அதை எழுத்துல கொடுக்க முடியுமா, அப்போ ரெண்டு பேருக்கும் தெளிவா இருக்கும்.
context: Asking for a verbal promise in writing.
explain: Asking for something 'in writing' avoids confusion. 'So' gives the reason.
usage: Use it after a phone call or talk when you need proof of what was agreed.
leelaQ: Why is it good to have agreements in writing?
answer: It avoids confusion and protects both people later.

en: If you can extend the warranty, we will place a bigger order.
tamil: நீங்க உத்தரவாதத்தை நீட்டிச்சா, நாங்க பெரிய ஆர்டர் கொடுப்போம்.
context: Trading a bigger order for a benefit.
explain: First conditional shows a deal: you give this, I give that.
usage: Use it to bargain with a seller or vendor.
leelaQ: What extra benefit would you ask for in a deal?
answer: I would ask for a longer warranty or free delivery.

en: What is the minimum quantity you can supply?
tamil: நீங்க கொடுக்கக்கூடிய குறைந்தபட்ச அளவு என்ன?
context: Asking a supplier about order size.
explain: 'Minimum' means the smallest amount allowed. 'Supply' means provide goods.
usage: Use it when you plan to order from a wholesaler or factory.
leelaQ: What would you ask a supplier before ordering?
answer: I would ask about the price, quantity and delivery time.

en: I need to check with my manager before I can confirm anything.
tamil: எதையும் உறுதி பண்றதுக்கு முன்னாடி என் மேனேஜர்கிட்ட கேக்கணும்.
explain: 'Check with' means ask for approval. It is a polite way to delay a decision.
usage: Use it when you are not allowed to decide alone.
leelaQ: What do you do when you cannot decide alone?
answer: I tell them I need to check with my manager first.

en: We are not in a position to accept those conditions right now.
tamil: இப்போதைக்கு அந்த நிபந்தனைகளை ஏத்துக்கிற நிலைமையில நாங்க இல்ல.
explain: 'Not in a position to' is a formal, polite way to say 'we cannot'.
usage: Use it in formal business replies when you must refuse.
leelaQ: How do you refuse something formally?
answer: I say we are not in a position to accept it.

en: I see your point, but I see it a little differently.
tamil: உங்க கருத்து புரியுது, ஆனா எனக்கு கொஞ்சம் வேற மாதிரி தோணுது.
explain: First accept the other view, then give yours with 'but'. It keeps the talk friendly.
usage: Use it when you disagree with a colleague without causing an argument.
leelaQ: How do you disagree politely?
answer: I first say I see their point and then share my view.

en: With respect, I am not sure that will work in practice.
tamil: மரியாதையோட சொல்றேன், அது நடைமுறையில வேலை செய்யும்னு எனக்கு உறுதியா தெரியல.
explain: 'With respect' softens a strong disagreement. 'In practice' means in real life.
usage: Use it with a senior person when you doubt their plan.
leelaQ: What do you say when an idea may not work?
answer: I say I am not sure it will work in practice.

en: That's a fair point, though I have one concern.
tamil: அது நியாயமான கருத்துதான், ஆனா எனக்கு ஒரு கவலை இருக்கு.
explain: 'Fair point' shows respect. 'Though' adds your different view in a soft way.
usage: Use it in a discussion to add a doubt without rejecting the idea.
leelaQ: What concern do you often raise at work?
answer: I often worry that we do not have enough time.

en: Have you considered the cost of doing it this way?
tamil: இப்படி பண்றதுக்கு ஆகுற செலவை யோசிச்சீங்களா?
explain: A question like this makes the other person think, instead of telling them they are wrong.
usage: Use it to challenge an idea politely in a meeting.
leelaQ: What would you ask before accepting a new plan?
answer: I would ask about the cost and the time needed.

en: I'm not sure I agree with that, but I'm open to discussing it.
tamil: அதுல எனக்கு உடன்பாடு இருக்கான்னு தெரியல, ஆனா அதை பேச நான் தயாரா இருக்கேன்.
explain: 'Open to' means willing to listen. It stops the conversation from becoming a fight.
usage: Use it when you want to disagree but keep a good relationship.
leelaQ: Are you open to changing your opinion?
answer: Yes, I am open if someone gives me a good reason.

en: Perhaps we could look at it from another angle.
tamil: ஒருவேளை நாம இதை வேற கோணத்துல பாக்கலாம்.
context: Suggesting a new way to think.
explain: 'Perhaps we could' is a soft suggestion. 'Angle' means a way of seeing a problem.
usage: Use it when a discussion is stuck.
leelaQ: How do you help when a discussion is stuck?
answer: I suggest looking at the problem from another angle.

en: I understand why you feel that way, but the data says otherwise.
tamil: நீங்க ஏன் அப்படி நினைக்கிறீங்கன்னு புரியுது, ஆனா தரவு வேற மாதிரி சொல்லுது.
explain: Showing understanding first, then facts, makes disagreement polite and strong.
usage: Use it in a meeting when numbers do not support someone's belief.
leelaQ: Do you trust data or feelings more?
answer: I trust data, but I also listen to people's feelings.

en: Could we agree to disagree on this one?
tamil: இந்த விஷயத்துல நாம வேறுபட்ட கருத்துலயே இருக்கலாமா?
explain: 'Agree to disagree' means accept that you have different opinions and stop arguing.
usage: Use it when a long argument is going nowhere.
leelaQ: When do you stop arguing about something?
answer: I stop when we both understand each other but still disagree.

en: Sorry to interrupt, but may I add something here?
tamil: இடையில பேசினதுக்கு மன்னிக்கணும், நான் இங்க ஒண்ணு சேர்க்கலாமா?
explain: 'Sorry to interrupt' is a polite opening. 'May I' asks for permission.
usage: Use it when you want to speak in a busy meeting.
leelaQ: How do you join a busy discussion?
answer: I say sorry to interrupt and ask if I may add something.

en: I don't think that is quite accurate, if you don't mind me saying so.
tamil: நீங்க தப்பா எடுத்துக்காட்டினா, அது சரியா இல்லன்னு நான் நினைக்கிறேன்.
explain: 'Not quite' is softer than 'wrong'. 'If you don't mind me saying' asks permission to be honest.
usage: Use it when you correct a fact said by a senior or a client.
leelaQ: How do you correct a mistake politely?
answer: I say it is not quite accurate and then give the right fact.

en: We might be better off waiting until next quarter.
tamil: அடுத்த காலாண்டு வரைக்கும் காத்திருந்தா நமக்கு நல்லதா இருக்கலாம்.
explain: 'Might be better off' is a soft way to advise. It does not sound like an order.
usage: Use it when you want to slow down a plan politely.
leelaQ: When is waiting the better choice?
answer: Waiting is better when we do not have enough money or time.

en: In short, the project is on track but the budget needs attention.
tamil: சுருக்கமா, திட்டம் சரியா போகுது, ஆனா பட்ஜெட்டுல கவனம் தேவை.
context: Summarising project status for a boss.
explain: 'In short' introduces a brief summary. 'On track' means going as planned.
usage: Use it to give a quick status update.
leelaQ: How is your work going this week?
answer: It is going well and I am on track to finish on time.

en: So, if I understand correctly, you want the report by Monday.
tamil: அப்போ, நான் சரியா புரிஞ்சிக்கிட்டா, உங்களுக்கு ரிப்போர்ட் திங்கள்கிழமைக்குள்ள வேணும்.
explain: This repeats the message in your own words to avoid mistakes.
usage: Use it after receiving instructions from a manager or client.
leelaQ: Why do you repeat instructions after you hear them?
answer: I repeat them to make sure I understood correctly.

en: The main point is that we need to reduce delays.
tamil: முக்கிய விஷயம் என்னன்னா, நாம தாமதங்களை குறைக்கணும்.
context: Stating the key message of a meeting.
explain: 'The main point is that' puts the key idea first. It is clear and easy to remember.
usage: Use it at the end of a long discussion to focus everyone.
leelaQ: What is the main point of your daily work?
answer: The main point is to help customers quickly and correctly.

en: To put it simply, customers want faster delivery and lower prices.
tamil: எளிமையா சொன்னா, வாடிக்கையாளர்களுக்கு வேகமான டெலிவரியும் குறைஞ்ச விலையும் வேணும்.
explain: 'To put it simply' tells the listener you are making a long idea short and easy.
usage: Use it to explain a long report to a non-expert.
leelaQ: What do your customers want most?
answer: They want good quality at a fair price.

en: Let me recap what we have agreed so far.
tamil: இதுவரை நாம ஒத்துக்கிட்டதை நான் திரும்ப சொல்றேன்.
context: Ending a meeting with a recap.
explain: 'Recap' means repeat the main points. It checks that everybody agrees.
usage: Use it at the end of a meeting before people leave.
leelaQ: What do you do at the end of a meeting?
answer: I recap the decisions and ask who will do what.

en: Can you summarise the main findings in two or three lines?
tamil: முக்கிய கண்டுபிடிப்புகளை ரெண்டு மூணு வரியில சுருக்கமா சொல்ல முடியுமா?
context: Asking a colleague for a short summary.
explain: 'Summarise' means give a short version. Giving a number of lines makes the request clear.
usage: Use it when you have no time to read a long document.
leelaQ: Can you summarise your day in two lines?
answer: I worked on a report and then attended two meetings.

en: Overall, the feedback was positive, with a few small suggestions.
tamil: மொத்தத்துல கருத்துகள் நேர்மறையா இருந்தது, சில சின்ன ஆலோசனைகளோட.
explain: 'Overall' gives the big picture. 'A few small suggestions' shows minor points.
usage: Use it to report feedback from customers or a review to your team.
leelaQ: What kind of feedback have you received at work?
answer: Most of it was positive and some was about small improvements.

en: Basically, we have two options: wait or start now.
tamil: அடிப்படையில, நமக்கு ரெண்டு வழி இருக்கு: காத்திருக்கலாம் இல்ல இப்போவே ஆரம்பிக்கலாம்.
context: Reducing a discussion to two choices.
explain: 'Basically' introduces the simple core of a long talk. Naming the options helps a decision.
usage: Use it when a discussion is long and the team must choose.
leelaQ: What two options do you have this weekend?
answer: I can rest at home or visit my relatives.

en: Here is what happened: the supplier was late, so we missed the deadline.
tamil: நடந்தது இதுதான்: சப்ளையர் தாமதம் பண்ணாரு, அதனால நாம காலக்கெடுவை தவறவிட்டோம்.
context: Explaining what went wrong in a few words.
explain: A colon introduces the explanation. 'So' shows the result of the cause.
usage: Use it when you explain a delay to your manager.
leelaQ: Have you ever missed a deadline? What happened?
answer: Yes, I missed one because the files were delayed.

en: The report covers sales, costs and our plans for next year.
tamil: அறிக்கையில விற்பனை, செலவுகள், அடுத்த வருஷ திட்டங்கள் இருக்கு.
explain: 'Covers' means includes the topic. Three items in a list sound complete.
usage: Use it to introduce a document to your team or boss.
leelaQ: What does your last report or document cover?
answer: It covers the work I did and the plan for next month.

en: Could you give me the short version? I only have two minutes.
tamil: சுருக்கமா சொல்ல முடியுமா? எனக்கு ரெண்டு நிமிஷம்தான் இருக்கு.
explain: 'The short version' means a brief explanation. Giving the reason makes the request polite.
usage: Use it with a colleague when you are busy.
leelaQ: What do you say when you are very busy?
answer: I say I only have two minutes and ask for the short version.

en: Sorry, could you explain what you mean by that?
tamil: மன்னிக்கணும், அதுக்கு என்ன அர்த்தம்னு விளக்க முடியுமா?
explain: 'What do you mean by' asks for the meaning. 'Sorry' makes it softer.
usage: Use it when you do not understand something at a meeting or class.
leelaQ: What do you do when you do not understand something?
answer: I politely ask the person to explain it again.

en: Just to be clear, do you want me to start today or tomorrow?
tamil: தெளிவுக்காக கேக்கறேன், நான் இன்னைக்கு ஆரம்பிக்கணுமா இல்ல நாளைக்கா?
explain: 'Just to be clear' introduces a question that avoids confusion.
usage: Use it when instructions are not complete.
leelaQ: Why is it good to ask a question when you are not sure?
answer: It avoids mistakes and saves time for everyone.

en: I'm not sure I followed that. Could you go over it once more?
tamil: எனக்கு அது புரியலன்னு தோணுது. இன்னொரு முறை சொல்ல முடியுமா?
context: Asking someone to repeat an explanation.
explain: 'Follow' means understand. 'Go over' means explain again.
usage: Use it in meetings, classes or phone calls when you got lost.
leelaQ: What do you say if you got lost in a talk?
answer: I say I did not follow and ask them to go over it again.

en: What I meant was that we should check the figures first.
tamil: நான் சொல்ல வந்தது என்னன்னா, முதல்ல எண்களை சரி பாக்கணும்.
explain: 'What I meant was' fixes a wrong understanding without blaming the listener.
usage: Use it when people misunderstand what you said.
leelaQ: How do you fix a misunderstanding?
answer: I calmly say what I meant and give an example.

en: Do you mean the old contract or the new one?
tamil: நீங்க பழைய ஒப்பந்தத்தை சொல்றீங்களா இல்ல புதுசையா?
explain: 'Do you mean' checks the meaning. Offering two options helps the person answer quickly.
usage: Use it when a colleague's words could mean two things.
leelaQ: What do you ask when you are confused about something?
answer: I ask which one they mean.

en: Let me rephrase that, because I don't think I was clear.
tamil: நான் தெளிவா சொல்லலன்னு நினைக்கிறேன், அதனால வேற மாதிரி சொல்றேன்.
context: Saying it again in a simpler way.
explain: 'Rephrase' means say it in different words. It takes the blame for the confusion.
usage: Use it when your listener looks confused.
leelaQ: How do you explain something in a simpler way?
answer: I use short sentences and simple words.

en: Could you give me an example so I can understand better?
tamil: நான் நல்லா புரிஞ்சிக்க ஒரு உதாரணம் சொல்ல முடியுமா?
explain: 'So I can' gives the reason. Examples make ideas easier to understand.
usage: Use it in a class, training or meeting.
leelaQ: Why are examples helpful when you learn?
answer: They make difficult ideas easy to see.

en: I'd like to confirm the meeting time, which I believe is three o'clock.
tamil: கூட்டத்தோட நேரம் உறுதி பண்ண விரும்பறேன், அது மூணு மணின்னு நினைக்கிறேன்.
context: Confirming a detail by email or phone.
explain: 'I'd like to confirm' is a polite way to check a detail. 'Which I believe' shows you are not fully sure.
usage: Use it before a meeting or visit to avoid a mistake.
leelaQ: What details do you confirm before a meeting?
answer: I confirm the time, the place and who is coming.

en: Which part of the process is unclear to you?
tamil: செயல்முறையில எந்த பகுதி உங்களுக்கு தெளிவா இல்ல?
explain: This question helps you find the exact problem. 'Unclear' means not easy to understand.
usage: Use it when you train or guide someone.
leelaQ: How do you help someone who is confused?
answer: I ask which part is unclear and explain only that.

en: Please let me know if anything in my message is not clear.
tamil: என் செய்தியில எதுவும் தெளிவா இல்லன்னா தயவுசெஞ்சு சொல்லுங்க.
explain: This line invites questions in a polite way. 'Let me know' means tell me.
usage: Use it at the end of an email or a long instruction.
leelaQ: What do you write at the end of an email?
answer: I write that I am happy to answer any questions.

en: I am writing to enquire about the position advertised on your website.
tamil: உங்க இணையதளத்துல விளம்பரம் செய்யப்பட்ட வேலையை பத்தி விசாரிக்க எழுதறேன்.
explain: 'I am writing to' is a standard formal opening. 'Enquire' means ask for information.
usage: Use it as the first line of a formal email.
leelaQ: Why do people write to companies?
answer: They write to ask for jobs, prices or information.

en: Thank you for your prompt reply to my previous email.
tamil: என் முந்தைய மின்னஞ்சலுக்கு உடனடியா பதில் அளிச்சதுக்கு நன்றி.
explain: 'Prompt' means quick. It is a polite thing to say in formal writing.
usage: Use it when a client or colleague answers quickly.
leelaQ: Who answers your messages quickly?
answer: My friend always replies within a few minutes.

en: Please find the attached document for your reference.
tamil: உங்க குறிப்புக்காக இணைக்கப்பட்ட ஆவணத்தை பாருங்க.
explain: 'Please find attached' is a common formal phrase when you send a file.
usage: Use it in office emails with files like reports or invoices.
leelaQ: What files do you send by email?
answer: I send reports, photos and forms.

en: I would be grateful if you could send me the details at your earliest convenience.
tamil: உங்களுக்கு வசதியான நேரத்துல விவரங்களை அனுப்பினா நன்றியா இருப்பேன்.
explain: 'I would be grateful if you could' is very polite. 'At your earliest convenience' means as soon as you can.
usage: Use it in formal emails to officers, clients or professors.
leelaQ: How do you make a formal request?
answer: I use words like I would be grateful if you could.

en: I apologise for the delay in getting back to you.
tamil: உங்களுக்கு பதில் சொல்ல தாமதமானதுக்கு மன்னிப்பு கேட்டுக்கறேன்.
explain: 'Apologise for' is followed by a noun or -ing form. It is formal and polite.
usage: Use it at the start of an email when you replied late.
leelaQ: When do you need to apologise at work?
answer: I apologise when I am late or forget something.

en: We regret to inform you that your order has been delayed.
tamil: உங்க ஆர்டர் தாமதமாகியிருக்குன்னு தெரிவிக்க வருத்தப்படறோம்.
context: Giving bad news to a customer.
explain: 'We regret to inform you' is a formal way to give bad news. 'Has been delayed' is passive.
usage: Use it in customer service emails or letters.
leelaQ: How do you tell a customer about bad news?
answer: I say sorry first and then explain what we will do.

en: I look forward to hearing from you soon.
tamil: உங்ககிட்ட இருந்து விரைவில் பதில் வரும்னு எதிர்பார்க்கிறேன்.
explain: 'Look forward to' is followed by an -ing form. It is a standard closing line.
usage: Use it as the last line of a formal email.
leelaQ: What do you look forward to this month?
answer: I look forward to meeting my family during the festival.

en: I would like to request a day's leave for personal reasons.
tamil: தனிப்பட்ட காரணங்களுக்காக ஒரு நாள் விடுப்பு கேக்க விரும்பறேன்.
context: Applying for leave from your manager.
explain: 'I would like to request' is a formal and polite way to ask. 'Personal reasons' needs no detail.
usage: Use it in a leave email to a manager or HR.
leelaQ: When do you ask for leave?
answer: I ask when I have a family function or I am unwell.

en: Could you kindly confirm receipt of this email?
tamil: இந்த மின்னஞ்சல் கிடைச்சதை தயவுசெஞ்சு உறுதி பண்ண முடியுமா?
context: Asking for a reply to confirm.
explain: 'Kindly' adds politeness. 'Confirm receipt' means say you have received it.
usage: Use it when you send an important document.
leelaQ: Why do you confirm that you received something?
answer: It shows the sender that the message arrived safely.

en: As discussed on the phone, I am sharing the revised proposal with you.
tamil: போன்ல பேசினபடி, திருத்தப்பட்ட முன்மொழிவை உங்களுக்கு அனுப்பறேன்.
explain: 'As discussed' links the email to an earlier talk. 'Revised' means changed or improved.
usage: Use it in an email after a phone call or meeting.
leelaQ: What do you send after an important call?
answer: I send a short email to confirm what we discussed.

en: Please do not hesitate to contact me if you need any further information.
tamil: மேலும் தகவல் வேணும்னா தயங்காம என்னை தொடர்பு கொள்ளுங்க.
explain: 'Do not hesitate to' means feel free to. It is a very common formal closing.
usage: Use it at the end of emails to clients and applicants.
leelaQ: Who can contact you when they need help?
answer: My students can contact me anytime when they need help.

en: Unfortunately, I will not be able to attend the meeting on Friday.
tamil: துரதிர்ஷ்டவசமா, வெள்ளிக்கிழமை கூட்டத்துல என்னால கலந்துக்க முடியாது.
explain: 'Unfortunately' softens bad news. 'Will not be able to' is a polite way to say 'cannot'.
usage: Use it when you must refuse an invitation or meeting.
leelaQ: How do you decline an invitation politely?
answer: I say unfortunately I cannot come and thank them for asking.

en: I have enclosed my resume and two reference letters.
tamil: என் ரெஸ்யூம் மற்றும் ரெண்டு பரிந்துரை கடிதங்களை இணைச்சிருக்கேன்.
context: Applying for a job by email.
explain: 'Enclosed' is formal for 'attached'. Present perfect shows the action is done now.
usage: Use it in a job application email.
leelaQ: What documents do you need for a job application?
answer: I need my resume, certificates and reference letters.

en: Would it be possible to reschedule our call to next Tuesday?
tamil: எங்க அழைப்பை அடுத்த செவ்வாய்க்கு மாத்த முடியுமா?
context: Asking to change a meeting time.
explain: 'Would it be possible to' is a polite, indirect way to ask for a change.
usage: Use it when you cannot keep an appointment time.
leelaQ: What do you say when you need to change a time?
answer: I ask if it would be possible to reschedule.

en: Thank you for your support, and I wish you all the best.
tamil: உங்க ஆதரவுக்கு நன்றி, உங்களுக்கு எல்லா நலனும் கிடைக்க வாழ்த்தறேன்.
context: Saying goodbye when leaving a job.
explain: 'I wish you all the best' is a warm, formal goodbye. It leaves a good impression.
usage: Use it in a farewell email to colleagues or a boss.
leelaQ: Whom would you thank when you leave a job?
answer: I would thank my manager and my team for their help.

en: What if we moved the launch to the first week of December?
tamil: நாம வெளியீட்டை டிசம்பர் முதல் வாரத்துக்கு மாத்தினா என்ன?
explain: 'What if' introduces a possible idea. It invites others to give opinions.
usage: Use it in a brainstorming session.
leelaQ: What idea would you suggest for your team?
answer: I would suggest a short meeting every Monday.

en: I have an idea that might save us some effort.
tamil: நமக்கு கொஞ்சம் உழைப்பை மிச்சப்படுத்தக்கூடிய ஒரு யோசனை என்கிட்ட இருக்கு.
context: Introducing an idea in a meeting.
explain: 'I have an idea' grabs attention. 'Might' shows you are not forcing it.
usage: Use it to share a suggestion with colleagues.
leelaQ: Have you ever had an idea that saved time?
answer: Yes, I used a checklist and it saved me a lot of time.

en: What do you think is the biggest risk with this approach?
tamil: இந்த அணுகுமுறையில மிகப்பெரிய ஆபத்து என்னன்னு நினைக்கிறீங்க?
context: Asking for opinions on a plan.
explain: Open questions like 'What do you think' invite detailed answers. 'Approach' means way of doing something.
usage: Use it in a planning meeting to hear everyone's view.
leelaQ: What risk do you worry about most?
answer: I worry that we may not have enough time.

en: It sounds good in theory, but I wonder how it will work in real life.
tamil: கோட்பாட்டுல நல்லா இருக்கு, ஆனா நிஜ வாழ்க்கையில எப்படி வேலை செய்யும்னு எனக்கு சந்தேகம்.
explain: 'In theory' and 'in real life' compare ideas with practice. 'I wonder' shows gentle doubt.
usage: Use it when an idea looks nice but you are unsure.
leelaQ: Is there an idea that sounds good but is hard to do?
answer: Yes, waking up at five every day is hard for me.

en: Let's brainstorm a few options before we choose one.
tamil: ஒண்ணை தேர்வு பண்றதுக்கு முன்னாடி சில வாய்ப்புகளை யோசிக்கலாம்.
explain: 'Brainstorm' means share many ideas quickly. 'Let's' invites the group to join.
usage: Use it when your team needs new ideas.
leelaQ: How does your team find new ideas?
answer: We sit together and share ideas without judging them.

en: Building on what Priya said, we could also offer a free trial.
tamil: பிரியா சொன்னதுல இருந்து, நாம இலவச சோதனையும் கொடுக்கலாம்.
explain: 'Building on' means adding to a previous idea. It shows respect for others.
usage: Use it in a meeting to connect your idea with another person's.
leelaQ: How do you respond to a good idea from a colleague?
answer: I thank them and add my own suggestion.

en: The advantage of this plan is that it costs very little.
tamil: இந்த திட்டத்தோட நன்மை என்னன்னா, இதுக்கு செலவு ரொம்ப கம்மி.
context: Explaining the benefit of an idea.
explain: 'The advantage of ... is that' is a clear way to list a benefit.
usage: Use it when you compare options in a meeting.
leelaQ: What is the advantage of your daily routine?
answer: It helps me finish all my work on time.

en: On the other hand, it could take longer than we planned.
tamil: மறுபக்கம், நாம திட்டமிட்டதை விட அதிக நேரம் எடுக்கலாம்.
context: Giving the downside of an idea.
explain: 'On the other hand' introduces a contrast. It helps you balance an argument.
usage: Use it in discussions after you mention a benefit.
leelaQ: What are the pros and cons of working from home?
answer: It saves travel time, but it can feel lonely.

en: How would this affect our current customers?
tamil: இது நம்ம தற்போதைய வாடிக்கையாளர்களை எப்படி பாதிக்கும்?
context: Asking about the impact of a decision.
explain: 'How would' asks about a possible result. 'Affect' is a verb meaning have an effect on.
usage: Use it to test an idea before a decision.
leelaQ: How would a new rule affect your work?
answer: It would change my routine and I would need time to adjust.

en: I haven't thought about that, but it's a really good question.
tamil: நான் அதை பத்தி யோசிக்கல, ஆனா அது ரொம்ப நல்ல கேள்வி.
explain: This buys you time and stays polite. 'Haven't thought about' uses present perfect.
usage: Use it when someone asks something you did not expect.
leelaQ: What do you say when you do not know the answer?
answer: I say it is a good question and promise to find out.

en: We should test the idea with a small group first.
tamil: நாம முதல்ல சின்ன குழுவோட இந்த யோசனையை சோதிச்சு பாக்கணும்.
explain: 'Should' gives advice. Testing small lowers the risk of a big mistake.
usage: Use it to advise a team before a big launch.
leelaQ: Why do people test an idea with a small group?
answer: It shows problems early before spending a lot of money.

en: Is this idea realistic given our current budget and timeline?
tamil: நம்ம தற்போதைய பட்ஜெட்டையும் காலக்கெடுவையும் வச்சு பாத்தா இந்த யோசனை நடைமுறைக்கு சாத்தியமா?
context: Questioning if a plan is practical.
explain: 'Given' means considering. 'Realistic' means possible in real life.
usage: Use it when you want to check an idea against limits.
leelaQ: What makes a plan realistic?
answer: It matches the money, time and people we have.

en: I think we are all on the same page now.
tamil: இப்போ நாம எல்லாரும் ஒரே கருத்துல இருக்கோம்னு நினைக்கிறேன்.
context: Checking agreement at the end of a discussion.
explain: 'On the same page' is an idiom meaning we all understand and agree.
usage: Use it at the end of a discussion before you move to action.
leelaQ: How do you make sure your team understands a plan?
answer: I ask everyone to repeat what they will do.

en: Don't worry, nobody will blame you for sharing a bad idea.
tamil: கவலைப்படாதீங்க, ஒரு மோசமான யோசனை சொன்னாலும் யாரும் உங்களை குறை சொல்ல மாட்டாங்க.
explain: 'Nobody' makes the sentence negative. It helps people feel safe to speak.
usage: Use it when you lead a team and want everyone to share ideas.
leelaQ: How do you help shy people speak up?
answer: I tell them every idea is welcome and ask them gently.

en: Could you walk me through your thinking on this?
tamil: இதை பத்தி நீங்க எப்படி யோசிச்சீங்கன்னு எனக்கு விளக்க முடியுமா?
explain: 'Walk me through' asks for a step-by-step explanation. It shows real interest.
usage: Use it when you want to understand a colleague's decision.
leelaQ: How do you ask someone to explain their decision?
answer: I ask them to walk me through their thinking.

en: Our priority this year should be improving customer service.
tamil: இந்த வருஷம் நம்ம முன்னுரிமை வாடிக்கையாளர் சேவையை மேம்படுத்தறதா இருக்கணும்.
context: Setting a direction in a planning meeting.
explain: 'Priority' means the most important thing. 'Should' gives a strong suggestion.
usage: Use it when you discuss goals for a team or a year.
leelaQ: What is your main priority this year?
answer: My main priority is to improve my English.

en: The more we discuss it, the clearer the solution becomes.
tamil: நாம எவ்வளவு பேசறோமோ அவ்வளவு தீர்வு தெளிவாகுது.
explain: 'The more..., the clearer...' is a pattern for two things that grow together.
usage: Use it to praise a useful team discussion.
leelaQ: When does talking help to solve a problem?
answer: Talking helps when everyone listens and shares honestly.

en: I'd rather take a little more time than make a hasty decision.
tamil: அவசர முடிவு எடுக்கறதை விட கொஞ்சம் அதிக நேரம் எடுத்துக்கறது எனக்கு பிடிக்கும்.
explain: 'I'd rather ... than ...' shows preference. 'Hasty' means done too quickly.
usage: Use it when someone pushes you to decide quickly.
leelaQ: Do you decide quickly or slowly?
answer: I prefer to think carefully before I decide.

en: Thanks for raising this; it is exactly what we needed to discuss.
tamil: இதை எழுப்பினதுக்கு நன்றி, நாம பேசவேண்டியது இதுதான்.
explain: Thanking someone for a point makes people more open. 'Raising' means bringing up a topic.
usage: Use it in a meeting when a colleague brings up an important point.
leelaQ: How do you thank someone for a useful comment?
answer: I say thanks for raising it and give my view.

en: Shall we set a clear deadline so nobody is confused later?
tamil: பின்னாடி யாருக்கும் குழப்பம் வராம இருக்க தெளிவான காலக்கெடுவை வைக்கலாமா?
explain: 'Shall we' is a polite suggestion. 'So' + clause gives the purpose.
usage: Use it near the end of a meeting to fix timelines.
leelaQ: Why do tasks need deadlines?
answer: Deadlines help us plan our time and finish the work.

en: The results have surprised everyone, including our own experts.
tamil: முடிவுகள் எல்லாரையும் ஆச்சரியப்படுத்திடுச்சு, எங்க சொந்த நிபுணர்களையும்.
explain: 'Including' adds an extra group. Present perfect shows a result that matters now.
usage: Use it when you talk about unexpected research or sales results.
leelaQ: What surprised you recently?
answer: The price of vegetables surprised me last week.

en: Let me think about it and get back to you by tomorrow evening.
tamil: நான் அதை யோசிச்சிட்டு நாளைக்கு சாயந்திரத்துக்குள்ள பதில் சொல்றேன்.
explain: 'Get back to you' means reply later. Giving a time shows you are serious.
usage: Use it when you cannot decide immediately.
leelaQ: What do you say when you need time to decide?
answer: I ask them to wait and say I will reply by tomorrow.
